STUDY · NEGATIVE RESULT · 11 OCT 2026
  We looked for the insider-buying edge in 470,754 Form 4 records and, outside 2008–09, did not find it.
  How small an effect this could have seen: with the crisis years removed, the 21-day excess return of insider-buying clusters has a 95% interval of [−0.26%, +0.62%]. A published 50 bp-a-month estimate sits inside that interval; an 82 bp estimate sits just outside it. Insider-buying signals are widely assumed to be large. This study was designed to find one.
  Published 11 Oct 2026 · Reviewed 17 Oct 2026 · Script: form4/ · Data: SEC Form 4 bulk files, 81 quarters, 2006–2026 Q1 · Originally at Substack · 2 pre-publication corrections, see Corrections
  Funding: none. No firm paid for, saw or approved this study. How donttrade is paid →
  Published whether or not the result was interesting. The script and data are linked above.

  What this is: I build trading tools and then publish the measurement, including when the measurement kills the idea. Methods and negative results, yes; live signals, never. It’s free — subscribing just means the next one finds you.When several company insiders buy their own stock in the same week, the stock tends to outperform. It is one of the better-documented anomalies in finance, it has a mechanism you can state in a sentence — the people who know most about a business are putting their own money into it — and it has been measured repeatedly over forty years.So I built the thing that reads those filings: all 81 quarterly SEC bulk files, 2006 through the first quarter of 2026, 470,754 records. Then, before trading it, I measured whether it still works.The honest answer is messier than “it doesn’t,” and the mess is the finding.The short versionIf you read nothing else:The signal is real in the data, and almost all of it is 2008 and 2009. Those two years supply 94% of the entire excess return of the era I would otherwise have called the one that worked.Take the crisis out and nothing is left. No stretch of years before 2017 shows a reliable gain once 2008–09 is removed.After 2017, in the stocks you could actually have bought, the average cluster trails the market — and not by enough to be sure of even that.In most cuts of this data the typical trade loses money — in both eras before any screen is applied, and on every cut after 2017, including the ones whose averages look impressive. A thin tail of large winners does the lifting.The year-to-year swing is several times larger than the effect anyone claims. Annual averages run from −2.85% to +5.80%, around claimed edges of well under one percentage point.So this is not an edge that decayed. It is a number too noisy to have been an edge in the first place — and a bug in my own code very nearly hid that from me.Everything below is the evidence, in order, with every figure checkable against a public repository. I have left in the places where the data argues against me, including two that are stronger than my own headline.What the literature saysIn one line, if you don’t need the citations: four independent studies, spanning forty years of data, all found that insider buying beats the market — and every one of their samples ends in 2016 or earlier.Kang, Kim and Wang (working paper, 2018) define a cluster as multiple insiders buying the same stock on the same or consecutive days, 1986–2016. At 21 trading days: cluster 3.80%, non-cluster 1.95%, a difference of 1.85% at t = 20.10. Those are DGTW characteristic-adjusted returns — benchmarked on size, book-to-market and momentum, not against an index.Twenty-one trading days is a month. That is a tradable horizon for someone who checks the market once a day.And unusually for an anomaly, the edge survives being long-only. Cohen, Malloy and Pomorski decompose it: for opportunistic insiders, equal-weighted, the long leg is 1.58% per month (t = 7.03) against a short leg of −0.23% that isn’t significant — my arithmetic makes that 87% of the spread. Their headline figure is more conservative: 82 basis points a month, value-weighted. Ali and Hirshleifer, across all insiders, get long 0.84% (t = 10.08) against short −0.03% (t = −0.64) — about 97% on the long side.But Ali and Hirshleifer also found the opposite where it is strongest, and it would be dishonest to cite them without it: among opportunistic insiders the short leg is −34 bp/month equal-weighted, −53 value-weighted, both significant at 1% — in their words, “in contrast with most previous work, the effect is substantial and significant even on the short side.” So the long-only story holds across insiders in general and weakens exactly where the signal is sharpest.Jeng, Metrick and Zeckhauser are cleanest: the purchase portfolio earns more than 50 basis points a month, and “the sale portfolio does not earn abnormal returns.” Insiders sell for a hundred reasons. They buy for one.Note the sample end dates. 2016. 2007. 2014. 1996.What I measuredThe SEC publishes every Form 4 as structured quarterly bulk files, free, back to 2006. I downloaded all 81 — 2006 Q1 through 2026 Q1. Every download succeeded.From those I kept open-market purchases only: transaction code P, shares acquired rather than disposed, blank and NONE tickers dropped, price and share count both positive.One correction to how this was described before. An earlier version of this pipeline claimed to exclude 10b5-1 plan transactions — pre-scheduled trades that carry no information about what an insider thinks today. It never did. The flag lives in the SEC’s SUBMISSION table and my code looked for it in the transactions table, where it does not exist in any of the 81 quarters, and the reader silently drops a column it cannot find. The filter is now applied where the field actually is. It exists only from 2023 Q1, covers 13 of 81 quarters, and removes 3.89% of filing-owner records in those quarters — 6.06% if you count individual transaction rows instead, and those two denominators are not interchangeable. That filter covers only the late era, so the two eras are not filtered alike.470,754 filing-owner records — not filings. The SEC’s reporting-owner table has one row per owner per filing, so a jointly filed Form 4 contributes more than one. That distinction turns out to matter and I come back to it.Then the signal. For each ticker in each calendar week of the filing date, I counted distinct SEC reporting-owner IDs and kept weeks with at least two and at least $100,000 of combined notional. Entry is the close of the first trading day after the last filing in that week — you cannot act on a filing before it exists. Hold 21 trading days. Benchmark is SPY over the identical window.That gives 66,874 cluster weeks, of which 35,888 clear the notional floor and 17,018 resolve to usable price data.One difference from the papers, stated up front. Kang, Kim and Wang measure from the transaction date. I measure from the filing date, because that is when the information is public and therefore when a reader could act. Post-SOX a Form 4 is due within two business days, so my window starts about two days later than theirs — and their own table shows 2.06% of the 3.80% accrues in the first five days. Starting late forfeits a large share of what they measure. That is most of why my magnitudes are smaller, and it is the honest version of the signal rather than the generous one.The result21-day market-adjusted return. The median is printed beside the mean wherever the two diverge enough to change what you would conclude, because that gap is most of this post:How to read the numbers in this postSkip this if you already know what a t-statistic is.21-day market-adjusted return — what the stock did over the next 21 trading days, about a calendar month, minus what SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, did over the exact same days. Positive means it beat the market.mean — the plain average across all the trades in that line. A portfolio earns the mean.median — the middle trade. Half did better, half did worse. A positive mean with a negative median means a few enormous winners are carrying a pile of losers.t — how sure you can be the number is not luck. Below about 2, it is indistinguishable from chance; above it, something is probably there.N — how many trades are in that line.cluster — one week in which two or more separate insiders at the same company filed purchases of its stock, totalling at least $100,000.as-traded price — the price the insider reported paying that day, rather than the retroactively adjusted price your charting software shows. Why that distinction matters is the section after this one.What the figures below are: all 17,018 clusters, with no screen for whether the stock was one you could realistically have bought.All clusters, ≥2 insiders: N 17,018 · mean +1.07% · median −0.76% · t 2.892006–2016: N 7,261 · mean +1.91% · median −0.21% · t 7.032017–2026 Q1: N 9,757 · mean +0.44% · median −1.27% · t 0.72Read the medians before the means. In the unscreened sample the median cluster loses money in both eras, including the one with a t of 7.03 — every positive figure there is a mean dragged up by a thin tail of large winners. That is not true once the liquidity and price screens are applied: in the early tradable universe the median is positive at every insider threshold (+0.06% at ≥2, +0.25% at ≥3, +0.30% at ≥4, +0.93% at ≥5 against a +1.54% mean). A portfolio earns the mean, so means are the right statistic for a trading claim — but a strategy whose median trade is negative is one you abandon long before the tail arrives, so I print both at the cuts the argument turns on.The screen that was wrong, and what fixing it didEvery “tradable” figure in v1 through v4 came from a filter that did not do what it said.The screen was price ≥ $5 and 20-day median dollar volume ≥ $1 million. The price came from Yahoo, and Yahoo’s closes are retroactively adjusted for splits. So Netflix’s 2006 insider buys — on $30 million a day of real volume — are recorded at a price of $0.29, because of splits in 2015 and 2025. Tesla’s 2011 cluster is recorded at $1.90. Both fail a $5 screen they cleared by two orders of magnitude at the time.Setting auto_adjust=False does not fix this; it only turns off the dividend adjustment. I checked: NVIDIA closed at about $1,208.88 on 7 June 2024, three days before a 10-for-1 split. Yahoo returns 120.54 adjusted and 120.89 unadjusted. There is no raw close to ask for.The fix was already in my own data and I had thrown it away. Form 4 reports TRANS_PRICEPERSHARE — the price the insider reported paying, on the transaction date, with no retroactive adjustment of any kind. My loader computed it, used it for the notional, and dropped it. Two different variables in this pipeline were called px, and the screen ran on the wrong one. (I say “reported paying” rather than “paid” deliberately — see the filing-errors section.)Re-screened on the as-traded price, Netflix 2006 is $19.99, Tesla 2010 is $17.00 and Tesla 2011 is $28.76. (Tesla 2010 is corrected but still excluded — it has no computable dollar volume, which is its own defect, below.) The dollar-volume half of the screen needed no change: the split adjustment cancels in price × volume, so those figures are as-traded up to a residual dividend-only deflation I have not measured.The error was not uniform across time, which is why it mattered. Among events that clear the liquidity floor — the only ones the price screen actually decides:What this is: how often the broken price screen made the wrong call, split by era. The mistake runs one way early and the other way late.2006–2016: wrongly admitted (px ≥ 5, real price < 5) 120 · wrongly rejected (px < 5, real price ≥ 5) 2522017–2026: wrongly admitted (px ≥ 5, real price < 5) 243 · wrongly rejected (px < 5, real price ≥ 5) 137Early on, forward splits deflate old adjusted prices and the screen threw out real companies. Recently, reverse splits inflate the adjusted prices of penny stocks and the screen let them in — ATRA’s November 2023 cluster shows an adjusted $12.03 against a real price of $0.24. The bias flips sign across exactly the two eras the post compares.Restricting to what you could actually buyBoth screens, so you can see what the correction did. As-traded is the specification I stand behind — the other is here because it produced every number I published before today.What this is: the result on stocks you could realistically trade — under the corrected price screen on the left, and the broken one that produced every number I published before today on the right.21-day:≥3 insiders, 2006–2016: as-traded (primary) +0.89% (t 2.70), median +0.25% · published spec (old) +0.99% (t 2.69), median +0.16%≥3 insiders, 2017–2026 Q1: as-traded (primary) −0.42% (t −1.33), median −1.16% · published spec (old) −0.58% (t −1.78), median −1.26%≥2 insiders, 2006–2016: as-traded (primary) +0.66% (t 3.01) · published spec (old) +0.59% (t 2.51)≥2 insiders, 2017–2026 Q1: as-traded (primary) −0.20% (t −0.86) · published spec (old) −0.30% (t −1.29)≥4 insiders, 2006–2016 / 2017–2026: as-traded (primary) +0.90% (t 2.13) / −0.29% (t −0.69)≥5 insiders, 2006–2016 / 2017–2026: as-traded (primary) +1.54% (t 3.21) / −0.64% (t −1.18)The two screens agree about 2,649 of the post-2017 events. On that common core the figure is −0.476% (t −1.48) — between the two, which is what you would hope for and not a result in its own right.Full sample post-2017: +0.44%. Tradable post-2017: −0.20%. The effect did not die everywhere — but the remainder is no longer significant either. Measured on the complement rather than asserted: non-tradable 2006–2016 +2.77% (t 6.41), non-tradable 2017–2026 +1.16% (t 0.91). It roughly halved and lost significance in the names you cannot practically buy; it went negative in the names you can.And now the thing I did not expectI removed 2008 and 2009 to check whether the good era leaned on the crash. Tradable, as-traded screen, with 95% confidence intervals, at both insider thresholds — because the two disagree and the stronger version is the one I was previously not printing:What this is: the early era with the crisis years taken out, at two levels of strictness for what counts as a cluster. This is where the title comes from.2006–2016: ≥2 insiders +0.66% (t 3.01), N 2,958 · ≥3 insiders +0.89% (t 2.70), N 1,524excluding 2008–09: ≥2 insiders +0.18% (t 0.80), median −0.14%, [−0.26, +0.62] · ≥3 insiders +0.06% (t 0.18), median −0.16%, N 1,178excluding 2008–09–10: ≥2 insiders +0.15% (t 0.62) · ≥3 insiders +0.02% (t 0.05), N 1,0732010–2016 only: ≥2 insiders +0.15% (t 0.58) · ≥3 insiders +0.14% (t 0.35), N 9462006–2007 only: ≥2 insiders +0.33% (t 0.73) · ≥3 insiders −0.25% (t −0.38), N 232None of those windows gets near significance; the largest t is 0.80, and at the tighter threshold the largest |t| is 0.38. Tradable with three or more insiders, 2008 was +3.17% (t 4.04, N 278, median +1.93%) and 2009 +5.80% (median +2.63%); nothing else in twenty-one years comes close. (2009 is 68 events with a 95% interval of [+0.94, +10.67]. It is the noisiest cell in the study and should not carry weight alone — the claim rests on 2008, which is 278 events at t 4.04.)2008 and 2009 supply 94% of the tradable, three-or-more-insider early era’s entire excess-return sum — 31% of the unscreened early era’s. Strip them and what remains of the tradable early era shows nothing significantly positive on any cut inside it.That last clause is doing real work and I want to be exact about how much. I enumerated every contiguous run of years in the sample with at least 30 events. Inside the early era, excluding 2008–09, no contiguous window reaches significance at three or more insiders — the largest |t| is 1.85 (2014 alone, N 143, −1.56%). At two or more insiders exactly one does: 2014–2015, −0.82% (t −2.13, N 709), and it is negative.It does not generalise past the early era. Across the full sample, 32 crisis-free contiguous windows reach nominal significance at three or more insiders and 41 do at two or more. They are overwhelmingly negative — 30 of 32 and 29 of 41 — and the strongest is 2021–2024 at −2.09% (t −4.79). But some are positive, and the honest ones to name are the ones that beat me:What this is: the calm stretches of years that look better than my own “good era.” I print them because they argue against me.crisis-free window, ≥2 insiders:2016–2018: N 1,238 · mean +1.10% · median +0.54% · t +3.412016–2019: N 1,679 · mean +0.89% · median +0.32% · t +3.202025–2026 Q1: N 821 · mean +2.36% · median −0.25% · t +3.05(my early-era headline, for comparison): N 2,958 · mean +0.66% · median +0.06% · t 3.012016–2018 and 2016–2019 — contiguous crisis-free runs straddling my own era break — are both more significant than the early era I am calling the one that worked. I am not going to pretend otherwise, and I am not going to claim it as a finding either: 231 contiguous windows are tested at each threshold, and a handful at t ≈ 3 out of 231 is what noise looks like. The 2025–2026 row has a negative median despite a +2.36% mean. (The counts are not an artefact of either cutoff: every one of the 231 windows clears the 30-event floor — the smallest is 65 events — and using exact per-degree-of-freedom critical values instead of a flat 1.96 changes none of them.)That is a failure to detect, not a proof of zero. The ex-crisis interval is [−0.26%, +0.62%] over 21 days. Jeng, Metrick and Zeckhauser’s lower bound of 50 bp a month sits inside it; Cohen, Malloy and Pomorski’s 82 bp sits just outside, so an effect of that size is about the smallest thing this window could have ruled out — and did. Anything smaller, this sample cannot speak to.If you’ve read this far: this is what every post here looks like — the finding, the thing that nearly fooled me, and the figures to check it with. Of these four, the crisis years are the two where the typical trade moved with the mean: 2008 +1.93% against +3.17%, 2009 +2.63% against +5.80%. The two nominally significant positive lines — 2025–2026 at t +2.05 and the pooled row at t +2.00 — both have a typical trade that loses money.All four of those lines are crisis-free, and three of the four are nominally significant — 2021–2024 at t −4.79, 2025–2026 at t +2.05, and the pooled row at t +2.00. The first points against the other two. That is the first thing to notice about them.Now put that last line where it belongs, next to the early era with its exceptional years removed, and with the medians this post promises everywhere else:What this is: the two eras side by side, each with its own exceptional years removed. On averages, the era I call dead is the stronger one.the era I say worked, crisis removed: N 1,178 · mean +0.06% · t 0.18 · median −0.16%the era I say died, four bad years removed: N 1,512 · mean +0.90% · t 2.00 · median −0.38%On means, the era I am calling dead is the stronger of the two. An earlier draft of this post printed the +0.90% on its own, called it the strongest argument against itself, and never set it beside the +0.06%. That omission was the worst thing in that draft.On medians the comparison does not merely fail to favour me — it reverses against the whole exercise. The typical trade in the “recovered” late era loses more than twice what the typical trade in the “working” early era loses. Neither pool has a positive median. Whatever these two numbers are evidence of, it is not that either period contained something you could have traded.The obvious rebuttal to the +0.90% is that nothing tells you in advance which regime you are in, so deleting 2021–24 is not something a trader could have done. That rebuttal is true, and it is weaker than it looks, because the two exclusions are not the same kind of thing. 2008–09 is a named macro event whose dates were fixed by history before anyone looked at this data. 2021–24 is four consecutive years selected because of their returns — the boundaries are the data. So I do not get to claim perfect symmetry, and an earlier draft of this post claimed it anyway.What I do get to say is narrower and, I think, more damaging to both numbers: this sample contains one two-year episode that supplies the entire positive mean and four years that supply the entire negative one, and the standard deviation of its annual mean is 2.05 percentage points. Remove either and the residue has a negative median. That is a description of variance, not of an effect.What this actually tells you is the point. The annual means run from −2.85% to +5.80% with a standard deviation of 2.05 percentage points, around effects being claimed at well under one point. The year-to-year noise is several times larger than the signal. Any era mean here is an average over sub-periods that disagree violently, and that is a better reason not to trade this than any single negative number.Did I choose the split that suited me?A fair question, since 2016/2017 is where the literature’s samples end and it is also where my story breaks. So I ran every single-year cut point.
